figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Latency per EM iteration against seven baselines on one NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB, four regimes, logarithmic axis, lower is better. A star marks the three configurations that fall back to Algorithm 3 because Algorithm 2 does not fit on chip; Algorithm 2 runs elsewhere. Axis-floor markers returned no valid fit, keyed in the legend; one such point, Flash-GMM at $K=4096$, is nonetheless discussed by latency in §5.3 and Appendix F as a disclosed exception to this criterion, so it is absent from this figure but present in those aggregate numbers. Protocol and validity criterion: §5.1; dispatch: §5.2.
figures.headline: Turbo-GMM is compared with seven baselines, with three fallback shapes starred and invalid fits drawn at the axis floor.
citing_sentences: Figure 1 compares Turbo-GMM against seven baselines.
The sweep covers sixteen shapes $(N,K,d)$ in four regimes—large $N$, large $K$, a $K/d$ sweep, and small $N$—one of which belongs to two, so Figure 1 shows seventeen bar groups.

Runs that fail the gate sit at the axis floor of Figure 1 and drop out of every memory and aggregate-count comparison below, with one disclosed exception: §5.3 and Appendix F keep and explicitly flag Flash-GMM’s $K=4096$ latency point even though it fails this gate, since a single E-step there is itself exact (Appendix G) and we would rather disclose a borderline inclusion than silently drop a data point that completed.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Cumulative mechanism ablation. Each bar adds one dataflow change to the ones below it; height is speedup over the Algorithm 1 dataflow, so the bars multiply and the dashed line is parity. The middle rung is not monotone: at $d=128$ our two-pass Algorithm 3 runs $17\times$ slower than not fusing, and only the one-pass Algorithm 2 recovers it—opposite in direction to the $17\times$ of §5.2, a loss of Algorithm 2 at $K=256$, $d=16$. A red $\times$ marks a rung that exceeds SRAM. Every rung agrees with the reference to $5\times 10^{-6}$; see §5.4.
figures.headline: At d=128 the two-pass form runs 17× slower than not fusing, and the single sweep recovers a net 1.46× over the standard dataflow.

abstract: Expectation-maximization (EM) for Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) requires scoring $N$ data points against $K$ mixture components. Prior fused GPU implementations, notably Flash-GMM, eliminate materialization of the $N\times K$ responsibility matrix but traverse the component dimension twice to compute normalization terms and accumulate sufficient statistics. We introduce Turbo-GMM, a single-sweep fused EM kernel that completes responsibility normalization and sufficient-statistic accumulation within one traversal of the component dimension. By retaining the complete component axis on chip, Turbo-GMM avoids the second score computation required by the released two-sweep Flash-GMM implementation. Its applicability is limited by register pressure, occupancy, and the component and feature dimensions, making it particularly suitable for large datasets with relatively small numbers of components. For larger configurations, Turbo-GMM employs a two-pass fallback following the established fused design. We establish algebraic equivalence to standard EM in real arithmetic and evaluate sixteen configurations on an NVIDIA A100. Under the reported benchmarking protocol, Turbo-GMM achieves a median $2.15\times$ speedup over the evaluated Flash-GMM implementation and up to $5.3\times$ and $9.9\times$ over PyTorch and scikit-learn, respectively. The results demonstrate the potential of single-sweep component traversal while identifying on-chip resource constraints as the principal limitation of this approach.

sections.body: Flash-GMM, the closest prior fused kernel, traverses the component dimension twice per EM iteration: once for the normalizers and again to recompute scores for the statistics. Turbo-GMM keeps the full component axis on chip beside a tile of points, so one traversal completes both reductions and the input tile is read once. This needs on-chip state proportional to $Kd$. The dispatch rule selects the single sweep when `K_pad` is at most 128 and `K_pad` times `d_pad` is at most 4096 on the evaluated A100, and otherwise uses a two-pass fallback. The authors call these implementation-specific thresholds, not hardware limits. Theorem 1 gives exactness in real arithmetic and Theorem 2 gives traffic under an explicit model. Across sixteen configurations, the median speedup over Flash-GMM is 2.15×.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Turbo-GMM fuses EM so one sweep over components completes responsibility normalization and statistic accumulation, removing a second score recomputation.

sections.body: The section fixes notation for $K$ diagonal Gaussians with weights $\pi$, means $M$ and variances $V$. The E-step forms the score matrix $S$ of log joint densities, then normalizes each row into responsibilities $\Gamma$ through row normalizers $L$. Lemma 1 writes the whole score matrix as one matrix product plus a per-component offset, the form libraries evaluate. The M-step reduces $\Gamma$ into soft counts, weighted first moments and weighted second moments. The archetype Algorithm 1 uses five kernels and writes and rereads $N\times K$ arrays. The authors state that its traffic counts follow from their definitions, not from profiled hardware counters, and that Algorithm 1 is not a transcription of any one library. The two reductions run on opposite axes: statistics sum over points, while the normalizer sums over components. This asymmetry sets the limit on fusion.
sections.heading: Background and the Standard Implementation
sections.headline: The baseline EM iteration expresses scores as one bilinear product, and its dataflow determines whether it can be fused.

sections.body: Algorithm 2 holds a block of rows and a block of components. When the component block covers all K components, one tile visit sees a full row of scores, so normalization finishes there and the E-step and M-step merge into one kernel. The kernel reads the input once and writes only the statistics. Padded columns get a finite sentinel of minus 3×10^38 instead of negative infinity, which would produce NaN. When K exceeds the component block, Algorithm 3 runs two passes: the first stores only row normalizers, and the second re-reads the data per component tile and recomputes the score. The authors name this extra read and recomputation as the cost Algorithm 2 avoids.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: Turbo-GMM completes normalization and statistic accumulation in one tile visit when the whole component axis fits on chip.

sections.body: Theorem 1 states that, in real arithmetic, both fused algorithms return the statistics and log-likelihood of standard EM for every row and component partition and every visit order. Tile sizes need not divide $N$ or $K$. The statistics fold over addition on the row axis, and the normalizer folds over the online-softmax merge on the component axis. The float32 kernel departs from these hypotheses: its sentinel mask holds only inside the single-precision exponent range, and where a component underflows it divides by $n_{k}$ plus ten float64 machine epsilons. The lifted score also loses relative accuracy far from the origin, so the data must be centered. Theorem 2 counts elements moved between memory and the chip, with atomic updates charged twice. Algorithm 2 moves $Nd+\Theta(PKd)$ elements, against $5Nd+6NK+\Theta(N+Kd)$ for Algorithm 1. Checks used a 60-decimal-digit reference.
sections.heading: Exactness and Cost
sections.headline: Both fused forms match standard EM in real arithmetic for any tiling and are costed under an explicit traffic model.

sections.body: Latency is measured at fixed quality: each arm's returned parameters are re-scored in double precision, and only finite fits with mixture weights summing to one are admitted. Turbo-GMM is faster than Flash-GMM on eleven of the fifteen shapes both complete, with a median 2.15× speedup. Against libraries the speedup reaches 5.3× over PyTorch and 9.9× over scikit-learn. Peak memory grows only from 128 to 139 MB as K rises from 128 to 4096, while materializing implementations use 3.2 to 47 GB. The single sweep alone reaches up to 19.4× over the authors' own two-pass fallback, and the Flash-GMM control at the same shape regresses by 2.07×. At $N=20\,000$ the method is slower than the best baseline, at 0.45× to 0.73×. Flash-GMM's K=4096 point fails the validity gate but is kept and flagged as a disclosed exception.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: On sixteen shapes, Turbo-GMM gives a median 2.15× speedup over Flash-GMM, with the advantage depending on on-chip residency.

sections.body: Online-softmax work supplies the merge rule that Algorithm 3 uses. Milakov and Gimelshein give the one-pass maximum and normalizer, Dao et al. make attention IO-aware, and Dao contributes the stored quantity from which a second pass recovers responsibilities. Bloch et al. fuse the EM iteration in Triton at the same traffic for the isotropic case. Their kernel sweeps the component axis twice and splits the sweeps across two launches, so the row normalizer returns to memory. Yang et al. fuse k-means assignment, the hard-assignment limit of the mixture case. Online and incremental EM methods reduce the number of outer passes over the data, which is orthogonal to the inner component pass removed here. GPU mixture libraries such as cuVS, scikit-learn, torchgmm, gmmx and pomegranate materialize a responsibility block, though a well-implemented library tiles the row axis to bound it.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior online-softmax and fused EM work supplies the merge rule and the two-sweep design; the single sweep is claimed to have no precedent.

sections.body: Peak memory is flat in the number of components, which changes what fits on one device. Latency is conditional: the one-pass form pays where the component axis fits on chip, which on the A100 means K at most 128 at d=32. The authors argue the binding resource is on-chip capacity, so the envelope may widen on later hardware, but they measure only one A100 and make no claim about other devices. cuVS is beaten at all sixteen shapes, by 2.2× rising to 70.6×, but the authors say that margin cannot be attributed to fusion alone. Scope is limited to diagonal covariances. The authors do not explain why the two-pass fallback loses to Flash-GMM at K=512 and K=1024. Algorithm 3 moves 3.4 GB at `(10^6, 512, 32)` in 11.9 ms, about a seventh of device bandwidth.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: The single sweep, not fusion alone, decides latency, and its benefit is bounded by on-chip capacity on one A100.

sections.body: The paper introduces Turbo-GMM, a fused EM implementation that avoids materializing the $N\times K$ responsibility matrix in every configuration. When the component axis fits on chip, it completes the E-step and M-step in one traversal. Theorem 1 gives exactness in real arithmetic under arbitrary tilings. Theorem 2 gives one-pass traffic of $\Theta(Nd+Kd)$ under the stated conditions. On sixteen configurations on one A100, the median speedup over the closest fused baseline is 2.15×, with up to 5.3× and 9.9× over PyTorch and scikit-learn. Peak memory is reduced by up to 338× relative to materializing implementations. Latency gains depend on residency and shape, while the memory saving also applies to the two-pass fallback.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Turbo-GMM avoids the responsibility matrix and completes EM in one traversal when the component axis fits, with latency gains conditional on shape.

sections.body: This appendix holds the AI usage disclosure, the two-pass construction, the proofs, and the Flash-GMM comparison. Appendix B derives the two-pass fallback with the online softmax merge and explains why a second pass is forced. Appendix C gives proofs of Lemma 1 and Theorem 1 and the term-by-term traffic accounting of Theorem 2. Appendix D holds the dispatch measurements, a latency and memory table at all sixteen shapes, and the ablation ladder. Appendix E lists library versions. Appendices F and G set the two constructions side by side and describe how Flash-GMM was benchmarked. The authors changed Flash-GMM's bf16 casts to tf32x3, fixed its row mask, and widened its autotune list. The widening moved the largest margin from 4.37× to 2.46×.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers usage disclosure, the two-pass construction, proofs, and the Flash-GMM benchmarking protocol.
